chapter_summary:
Perception is the bridge between the physical world and the robot's internal model of that world. While humans rely primarily on vision, robots can use many sensors: cameras, LiDAR, radar, sonar, infrared, and tactile sensors. In this module, we focus on **computer vision** — the use of cameras to extract geometric and semantic information about the environment. Cameras are the most common perception sensor in robotics because they are cheap, lightweight, passive (do not emit energy), and provide rich information (color, texture, shape).

The foundation of computer vision is the **pinhole camera model**. A pinhole camera is a dark box with a tiny hole (aperture) that allows light to enter. Light from a point in the world passes through the pinhole and projects onto the image plane on the opposite side of the box. The image is inverted, but the geometry is simple and well-defined.

The **perspective projection equation** relates a 3D point in the world `P = [X, Y, Z]^T` to its 2D projection `p = [u, v]^T` on the image plane:

```
u = f * X / Z + cx
v = f * Y / Z + cy
```

Where `f` is the focal length (distance from the pinhole to the image plane), and `(cx, cy)` is the principal point (the intersection of the optical axis with the image plane). This equation tells us that the apparent size of an object in the image is inversely proportional to its distance from the camera. A object that is twice as far away appears half as large.

In homogeneous coordinates, the projection can be written as a matrix multiplication:

```
[u]   [f  0  cx]   [X]
[v] = [0  f  cy] * [Y]
[1]   [0  0  1 ]   [Z]
```

The 3×3 matrix is called the **intrinsic matrix** (or camera matrix) and is denoted `K`. It contains the **intrinsic parameters** of the camera: focal length `f`, principal point `(cx, cy)`, and (for non-square pixels) the pixel aspect ratio. These parameters are fixed for a given camera and lens and do not change when the camera moves.

The **extrinsic parameters** describe the position and orientation of the camera in the world. They are represented by a rotation matrix `R` and a translation vector `t`, which together form the homogeneous transformation `T = [R | t]`. The full projection from a world point `P` to an image point `p` is:

```
p_homogeneous = K * [R | t] * P_homogeneous
```

Or in expanded form:

```
[u]     [f  0  cx]   [r11 r12 r13 t1]   [X]
[v]  =  [0  f  cy] * [r21 r22 r23 t2] * [Y]
[1]     [0  0  1 ]   [r31 r32 r33 t3]   [Z]
                                      [1]
```

This is the fundamental equation of camera geometry. It has 6 extrinsic parameters (3 for rotation, 3 for translation) and 5 intrinsic parameters (f, cx, cy, and two distortion coefficients). To use a camera for robotics, we must first **calibrate** it — estimate the intrinsic parameters and, if necessary, the distortion coefficients.

**Camera calibration** is typically done using a checkerboard pattern. The checkerboard has known dimensions, and its corners are easy to detect in images. By taking images of the checkerboard from different viewpoints, we obtain a set of 3D-2D correspondences. These correspondences are used to solve for the intrinsic parameters using an optimization algorithm (like the Zhang method or a nonlinear least-squares solver).

In MATLAB, camera calibration is done with the Computer Vision Toolbox:

```matlab
% Detect checkerboard corners in a set of images
imageFiles = dir('calibration_images/*.jpg');
images = cell(1, length(imageFiles));
for i = 1:length(imageFiles)
    images{i} = imread(fullfile(imageFiles(i).folder, imageFiles(i).name));
end

% Detect corners
[imagePoints, boardSize] = detectCheckerboardPoints(images);

% Generate world coordinates of the corners
squareSize = 25; % mm
worldPoints = generateCheckerboardPoints(boardSize, squareSize);

% Calibrate the camera
[cameraParams, imagesUsed, estimationErrors] = estimateCameraParameters(...
    imagePoints, worldPoints, 'ImageSize', size(images{1}, [1 2]));

% Display results
display(cameraParams);
```

**Lens distortion** is a deviation from the ideal pinhole model caused by the lens. Real lenses introduce two types of distortion:
- **Radial distortion:** Straight lines appear curved, especially near the edges of the image. This is caused by the lens having a different focal length at different distances from the optical center. It is modeled as: `x_distorted = x * (1 + k1*r² + k2*r⁴ + k3*r⁶)`.
- **Tangential distortion:** The image plane is not perfectly parallel to the lens, causing points to be shifted tangentially. Modeled as: `x_distorted = x + [2*p1*x*y + p2*(r² + 2*x²)]`.

The distortion coefficients `(k1, k2, k3, p1, p2)` are estimated during calibration and used to undistort images:

```matlab
undistortedImage = undistortImage(originalImage, cameraParams);
```

Undistortion is essential for accurate 3D reconstruction, visual odometry, and any application that relies on precise geometric measurements from images.

screens.title: Camera Models and Projective Geometry
screens.subtitle: How a camera turns a 3D scene into a 2D image and why accurate geometry matters for robotics

narration.text: In this chapter we connect the physical camera to the equations robots use to understand the world. You will learn the pinhole camera model, the perspective projection equation, the intrinsic camera matrix, and how rotation and translation place a camera in the world. We also cover camera calibration with a checkerboard and two common lens distortions that must be corrected. These are not abstract details: a robot that must localize, measure distances, or build 3D maps depends on accurate camera geometry. For example, measuring the distance to an object from pixel coordinates requires the focal length and principal point. We will show how calibration recovers those numbers from images, and why uncorrected distortion bends straight lines and undermines pose estimation. By the end of this lesson you will be able to state the projection equation, explain the roles of intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, and describe the basic calibration workflow. Consider a simple use case: a manipulator using an uncalibrated camera will misplace a pick by a persistent bias. That practical gap is why calibration and undistortion are essential. What would happen to your robot's measurements if the focal length were wrong?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A camera maps 3D points to 2D via a projection defined by intrinsic parameters (K) and extrinsic pose ([R|t]); calibration and undistortion recover the numbers robots need for accurate geometry.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Camera Models
Camera Models and Projective Geometry
Understand how 3D scenes become 2D images and why calibration is essential for precise measurement.
In this lesson
Pinhole model, projection equation, K matrix, extrinsics, calibration, and distortion.
Why it matters
Robots use calibrated cameras to measure distances, estimate pose, and build accurate 3D maps.
Practical check
Try projecting a known 3D point with given f and cx, cy to verify your calibration numerically.
Common pitfall
Using raw images without undistortion leads to curved lines and biased feature locations in geometry estimates.
Getting started

Follow the upcoming screens: core equations, a calibration workflow, a MATLAB code walkthrough, and distortion correction. Each step connects the math to practical checks you can run on a webcam.

Visual concept
Pinhole geometry + pipeline
A compact visual: 3D points pass through a pinhole and form an inverted image. We convert that geometry into algebraic matrices for robotics.
Explore key topics
Projection equation and intuition for scale with distance.
Calibration with checkerboards to recover intrinsic parameters.
Lens distortion models and undistortion for accurate geometry.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In the first group of objectives, we focus on building a precise vocabulary and measurable skills. You will model the pinhole camera and explain the perspective projection equation so you can predict where a 3D point will appear in an image. You will distinguish intrinsic parameters, which are fixed properties of the camera and lens, from extrinsic parameters, which describe the camera's pose in space. Being able to state these definitions clearly matters because algorithms for pose estimation, structure from motion, and visual odometry depend on them. A simple example: if you know the focal length and principal point you can map a known 3D coordinate to pixel coordinates and check your math. A common misconception is to treat focal length as a single scale without acknowledging the principal point offset or pixel aspect ratio. Each objective here is a competency you can verify with short calculations or visual checks. These skills form the foundation for calibration, undistortion, and reliable geometric reasoning with camera images.

keyIdea.title: Focus
keyIdea.text: Define pinhole and projection; separate camera-internal parameters from external pose so later calibration and undistortion make sense.

narration.text: The second set of objectives moves from definitions to hands-on validation and error awareness. You will run a calibration routine with multiple images of a checkerboard and interpret the outputs: focal length in pixels, principal point, and distortion coefficients. A concrete example is taking ten images at varied angles and confirming that detected corner re-projection errors are small—this validates your estimate. You will use undistortion to remove radial and tangential effects and verify results by checking that straight grid lines are straight after correction. Another important skill is understanding typical failure modes: insufficient viewpoint variation, poor corner detection, or too few images lead to weak calibration. You will learn to check imagesUsed and estimationErrors, and to visually compare original and undistorted images. These objective-driven checks give you measurable criteria to decide whether the camera parameters are ready for use in mapping, pose estimation, or any task that requires geometric accuracy.

screens.title: Perception and the role of cameras
screens.subtitle: Why cameras are central sensors in robotics

narration.text: Perception links sensors to a robot's internal model of the world, and cameras are among the most widely used sensors because they are passive, lightweight, and rich in information. The camera gives color, texture, and shape cues that are essential for recognizing objects, estimating depth, and planning actions. Define the camera here as a geometric device: it maps rays of light from the world into a 2D array of pixels. This mapping can be described with simple geometry and matrices, which is why cameras are so useful for computation. A concrete example: a mobile robot detecting a door uses image features; to calculate the door's distance and orientation from the robot, the robot needs the camera's projection parameters. A common misconception is thinking a camera itself measures depth directly; it does not — depth must be inferred by geometry, stereo, or motion. The practical takeaway is this: when you treat the camera as a geometric instrument with known parameters, you can convert pixel observations into meaningful spatial estimates. How will you check that your camera is behaving like a reliable geometric instrument?

keyIdea.title: Why cameras
keyIdea.text: Cameras are rich, passive sensors whose outputs become meaningful when combined with geometric models and calibration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Perception
Definition
A camera maps rays from 3D world points to a 2D pixel grid. This process is geometric and described by projection equations and matrices used in robotics.
Concrete example
A mobile robot estimates a door's distance by projecting door corner coordinates into image pixels and solving for depth using known focal length.
Misconception
A single camera does not measure depth without geometry. Depth must be inferred from scale, stereo, or motion.
Key Takeaway

Treat cameras as calibrated geometric instruments to convert pixels into spatial information for perception tasks.

Analogy
Think of a camera as a window with a fixed magnifying glass: the view is rich but you must know the glass properties to measure sizes and distances behind it.
Why this fills the robot's needs
  • Rich visual features for recognition and localization.
  • Geometry lets you turn pixels into metric estimates with calibration.
  • Calibration and undistortion remove systematic biases for accurate mapping.

screens.title: The Pinhole Camera Model
screens.subtitle: A simple geometric model that yields the perspective projection

narration.text: The pinhole camera is a compact geometric model: imagine a light-tight box with a single small aperture. A point in the world projects through the pinhole and traces a straight line to the image plane, producing an inverted image. Formally, for a 3D point P = [X, Y, Z]^T, the image coordinates follow u = f X / Z + cx and v = f Y / Z + cy, where f is the focal length and (cx, cy) is the principal point. This equation captures a key intuition: apparent size scales inversely with depth. A concrete numeric example makes this clear: with focal length f = 500 pixels and a point at Z = 5 meters, the X coordinate at 2 meters projects to u = 500 * 2 / 5 + cx. A common misunderstanding is treating focal length as distance in meters; in image processing it is often expressed in pixels because it combines physical focal length and pixel scaling. The practical test is simple: move an object away and watch its image size shrink proportionally. That observation is the geometric basis for depth cues in monocular vision and the starting point for calibration and pose estimation.

keyIdea.title: Pinhole intuition
keyIdea.text: Apparent size is inversely proportional to distance; the projection equation encodes that relation and introduces focal length and principal point.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Pinhole Model
Equation
The central projection is u = f X / Z + cx, v = f Y / Z + cy. It tells how 3D coordinates map to pixel locations given camera internals.
u = f * X / Z + cx
v = f * Y / Z + cy
Concrete check
If f=500px, cx=320, cy=240 and P=[2,1,5], then u=520, v=340. Use this to validate estimated f and principal point.
Visual intuition
As Z grows, X/Z and Y/Z shrink. That inverse relation is the reason objects appear smaller the farther they are from the camera.
Misconception
Focal length is not always a physical millimeter distance in image processing; it is commonly expressed in pixels after combining with pixel pitch.
Key Takeaway: Use the projection equation to test and validate calibration numerically.

screens.title: Intrinsic Matrix K
screens.subtitle: Packaging focal length and principal point into a 3×3 matrix

narration.text: The intrinsic matrix K packages the camera's internal parameters into a concise 3×3 matrix used in matrix multiplication for projections. In its simple square-pixel form it looks like K = [[f, 0, cx], [0, f, cy], [0, 0, 1]]. Using homogeneous coordinates this lets us write the projection as a single matrix multiply, which is convenient for chaining transforms. The entries f, cx, and cy are measured in pixels: f embodies focal length scaled by pixel size, and (cx, cy) marks the principal point where the optical axis meets the image plane. A concrete example is forming K with f=500 and cx=320, cy=240 and multiplying K by a camera-coordinate vector to obtain homogeneous image coordinates. A common oversight is forgetting the pixel aspect ratio or skew if pixels are rectangular or the sensor is misaligned; in that case K has additional terms. The practical reason we use K is to combine focal scale and principal point into one operator so the projection fits neatly into linear algebra pipelines used by robotics and vision systems. Intrinsic Matrix K means k combines focal length and principal point into a 3×3 matrix so projection becomes a matrix multiplication in homogeneous coordinates.. In practical terms, packaging focal length and principal point into a 3×3 matrix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: K groups internals
keyIdea.text: K combines focal length and principal point into a 3×3 matrix so projection becomes a matrix multiplication in homogeneous coordinates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Intrinsic Matrix
Matrix form
K = [ f  0  cx
      0  f  cy
      0  0  1 ]
K maps camera coordinates to pixel coordinates when used with homogeneous vectors, making projection linear in the homogeneous representation.
Concrete example
With f=500, cx=320, cy=240, multiply K by [X, Y, Z]^T and scale by 1/Z to retrieve u,v in pixels for validation.
Notes and pitfalls
If pixels are not square, K includes pixel aspect ratio; if the sensor is skewed there is an extra off-diagonal term. Most algorithms assume the simple form, so inspect your camera metadata.
Why this matters
K is the interface between raw pixel readings and metric camera geometry. Accurate K is required for mapping image measurements into metric space.

screens.title: Extrinsic Parameters — R and t
screens.subtitle: Describing camera position and orientation in the world

narration.text: Extrinsic parameters describe where the camera is situated and how it is rotated relative to the world coordinate frame. They are represented by a rotation matrix R and a translation vector t. Together they transform a world point P_world into camera coordinates: P_camera = R * P_world + t. This matters because K alone assumes coordinates are in the camera frame; to project a general world point you must first bring it into camera space with R and t. A concrete example: if a camera is translated one meter forward and rotated down by 10 degrees, R and t express that pose and change projected pixel coordinates accordingly. A common misconception is to treat R and t interchangeably with camera intrinsic parameters — they are not: extrinsics vary as the camera moves. The practical usage is to form the 3×4 matrix [R | t], combine it with K to get the full projection matrix, and use it to map world coordinates to pixels for tasks such as augmented reality or object localization. Extrinsic Parameters — R and t means r and t place the camera in the world so world points can be transformed into camera coordinates before projection by k.. In practical terms, describing camera position and orientation in the world. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pose matters
keyIdea.text: R and t place the camera in the world so world points can be transformed into camera coordinates before projection by K.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Extrinsic Parameters
Transform
World to camera: P_cam = R * P_world + t. R rotates, t translates. Together as [R | t] they convert world homogeneous coordinates to camera homogeneous coordinates.
Example
A camera 1m forward and pitched down changes the Z coordinate of points relative to the camera, altering their projected u and v values.
Common pitfall
Mixing camera and world frames without applying R and t leads to incorrect projections. Always transform world points into camera coordinates first.
Key Takeaway
Extrinsics are the moving part of the projection pipeline. They must be estimated or known to place image measurements into the world.

screens.title: Full Projection Pipeline: p = K [R | t] P
screens.subtitle: Combining internals and pose into a single projection equation

narration.text: The full projection pipeline composes the extrinsic transform with the intrinsic matrix: p_homogeneous = K * [R | t] * P_homogeneous. In practice this means you first convert a world point to camera coordinates using R and t, then apply K to scale and offset into pixel space, and finally normalize by the homogeneous scale to get (u, v). This pipeline is the fundamental equation of camera geometry and is used in everything from pose estimation to 3D reconstruction. A concrete walkthrough: take a 3D world point, multiply by the 3×4 matrix [R|t] to obtain a 3-vector in camera coordinates, then multiply by K to get a homogeneous image vector, and divide by its third coordinate to obtain pixel coordinates. A common mistake is to forget the final division by Z when converting from homogeneous coordinates, which leaves coordinates unnormalized and incorrect. The practical implication is that every algorithm that uses image points for metric tasks depends on this order of operations—mixing them up will undermine mapping and localization. Full Projection Pipeline: p = K [R | t] P means transform world points to camera coordinates with [r|t], apply k, then normalize by depth to get pixel coordinates.. In practical terms, combining internals and pose into a single projection equation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline order
keyIdea.text: Transform world points to camera coordinates with [R|t], apply K, then normalize by depth to get pixel coordinates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Full Projection
Pipeline (algebra)
p_homogeneous = K * [R | t] * P_homogeneous
Then u = p_homogeneous(1) / p_homogeneous(3)
     v = p_homogeneous(2) / p_homogeneous(3)
This sequence—transform then project then normalize—is the canonical flow used in vision algorithms for reprojection and error computation.
Misstep to avoid
Omitting the normalization step leaves coordinates scaled by depth and will produce incorrect image locations for comparisons.
Concrete scenario
Use this pipeline to reproject known world landmarks and compute reprojection error during calibration. Small reprojection error means your estimated K, R, and t are consistent with observed corners.
Key Takeaway
The chained transform is the single mathematical statement that all camera geometry relies upon; keep the order correct and always normalize.

screens.title: Camera Calibration with Checkerboards
screens.subtitle: Collecting corner correspondences and solving for intrinsics

narration.text: Camera calibration estimates a camera's intrinsic parameters and often distortion coefficients from images of a known pattern—commonly a checkerboard. The process has clear steps: capture many images of the board at varied poses, detect corner points in each image, generate corresponding world coordinates for board corners, and solve for the intrinsic parameters with an optimization that minimizes reprojection error. A concrete example: print a board with squareSize=25 millimeters, record 10–15 images from different angles, and use detected imagePoints with known worldPoints to run an estimate routine. Important practical advice: vary the viewpoints and distances so corners cover the full image area; this reduces extrapolation errors at the edges. A common misconception is that more images automatically mean better calibration—quality and diversity matter more than quantity. The final validation step is to check mean reprojection error and visually compare original and undistorted images; small errors and straightened grids indicate a good fit. This process is the industry standard for preparing cameras for metric perception. Camera Calibration with Checkerboards means capture diverse checkerboard views, detect corners, generate world points, and optimize parameters to minimize reprojection error.. In practical terms, collecting corner correspondences and solving for intrinsics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calibration steps
keyIdea.text: Capture diverse checkerboard views, detect corners, generate world points, and optimize parameters to minimize reprojection error.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Calibration
Step-by-step
1
Capture 10–15 images of a checkerboard at varied angles and distances to cover the image plane.
2
Detect corner points in each image to get imagePoints and boardSize.
3
Generate worldPoints from boardSize and squareSize to create correspondences.
4
Run an optimization to estimate K and distortion coefficients and inspect reprojection error.
Validation
Look at mean reprojection error and visually compare original vs undistorted images. Straightened grid lines indicate successful undistortion.
Practical tip
Avoid shots where checkerboard fills only a corner; ensure the pattern appears at multiple scales and rotations.
Common mistake
Using near-identical, small viewpoint changes yields unstable parameters even with many images because the data lacks informative variation.

screens.title: MATLAB Calibration Code Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Detecting corners and estimating camera parameters

narration.text: Here we walk through a typical MATLAB calibration script to connect the math to runnable steps. First, load a set of images from a folder. Next, use detectCheckerboardPoints to find corner image coordinates and boardSize; generateCheckerboardPoints produces worldCoordinates using the known square size. Lastly, estimateCameraParameters solves for cameraParams, imagesUsed, and estimationErrors. A concrete example: use squareSize = 25 millimeters, and pass the imagePoints plus worldPoints to estimateCameraParameters specifying the ImageSize. After calibration, display(cameraParams) summarizes focal length, principal point, and distortion. A common confusion is reading focal length units—MATLAB reports focal length in pixels when imageSize is provided. For validation, inspect imagesUsed to ensure all images were accepted and look at mean reprojection error in estimationErrors. UndistortImage applies the computed camera parameters to correct an image. The practical takeaway is to run this pipeline on your dataset, verify reprojection errors are low, and visually compare undistorted and original images to confirm straightening of lines. MATLAB Calibration Code Walkthrough means load images, detect checkerboard corners, generate world points, call estimatecameraparameters, inspect errors, and undistort images.. In practical terms, detecting corners and estimating camera parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MATLAB flow
keyIdea.text: Load images, detect checkerboard corners, generate world points, call estimateCameraParameters, inspect errors, and undistort images.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › MATLAB Walkthrough
Representative code
% Detect checkerboard corners in a set of images
imageFiles = dir('calibration_images/*.jpg');
images = cell(1, length(imageFiles));
for i = 1:length(imageFiles)
    images{i} = imread(fullfile(imageFiles(i).folder, imageFiles(i).name));
end

% Detect corners
[imagePoints, boardSize] = detectCheckerboardPoints(images);

% Generate world coordinates
squareSize = 25; % mm
worldPoints = generateCheckerboardPoints(boardSize, squareSize);

% Calibrate
[cameraParams, imagesUsed, estimationErrors] = estimateCameraParameters(...
    imagePoints, worldPoints, 'ImageSize', size(images{1}, [1 2]));

% Display results
display(cameraParams);
Explanation
detectCheckerboardPoints finds imagePoints; generateCheckerboardPoints creates metric worldPoints using the square size. estimateCameraParameters runs the optimization and returns cameraParams containing f, cx, cy and distortion coefficients.
Validation tips
Check imagesUsed for rejected images, inspect estimationErrors for large values, and undistort an image to visually confirm straightened lines.

screens.title: Lens Distortion — Radial
screens.subtitle: Why straight lines curve and how radial distortion is modeled

narration.text: Radial distortion bends straight lines, usually in a symmetric pattern around the optical center, and is caused by lens elements having different focal lengths across the field. It is commonly modeled by a polynomial factor: x_distorted = x * (1 + k1 r^2 + k2 r^4 + k3 r^6), where r is the radius from the principal point. A concrete example: a straight grid photographed with a wide-angle lens exhibits barrel distortion—lines bow outward near edges. Calibration estimates coefficients k1, k2, k3 so we can remove this effect numerically. A typical misconception is to apply a single coefficient and assume all curvature is fixed; in practice multiple terms may be needed for strong distortions. Practically, after estimating these coefficients you apply an undistortion mapping that moves pixel samples so straight lines reappear straight. This correction is essential for tasks like 3D reconstruction or visual odometry, because distorted measurements produce systematic geometric errors that propagate into metric estimates. Lens Distortion — Radial means radial terms multiply coordinates by a polynomial in radius; calibration estimates k1,k2,k3 so images can be corrected and geometry restored.. In practical terms, why straight lines curve and how radial distortion is modeled. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Radial distortion
keyIdea.text: Radial terms multiply coordinates by a polynomial in radius; calibration estimates k1,k2,k3 so images can be corrected and geometry restored.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Radial Distortion
Model
x_distorted = x * (1 + k1*r^2 + k2*r^4 + k3*r^6)
where r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
This multiplicative factor increases with radius and bends straight lines away from the center for barrel distortion or inward for pincushion distortion depending on sign.
Example and check
Photograph a printed grid. If grid lines curve near the edge, radial distortion is present. After estimating k1..k3, undistort the image and verify lines are straight.
Common pitfall
Using too few radial terms can leave residual curvature; use as many terms as needed to fit the observed bending during calibration.

screens.title: Lens Distortion — Tangential
screens.subtitle: Sensor alignment errors and the tangential distortion model

narration.text: Tangential distortion arises when the lens and the image plane are not perfectly parallel, producing shifts that are not radially symmetric. The model uses two parameters p1 and p2 and adjusts coordinates like x_distorted = x + [2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2)]. This term accounts for decentering or tilt of lens elements relative to the sensor. A concrete scenario is when an inexpensive lens is mounted slightly tilted; straight lines can appear slanted asymmetrically across the image. During calibration both radial and tangential coefficients are estimated together because they both affect detected corner positions. A common misconception is that tangential error is negligible; while small for well-built optics, it can be significant for cheap lenses or poor mechanical mountings. Practically, undistortion uses the full set of coefficients k1,k2,k3 and p1,p2 to remap pixels to corrected positions so downstream geometric computations see straight lines and consistent samplings. keyIdea.text: Tangential distortion models decentering of lens elements with p1 and p2; include them in calibration when sensor-lens alignment is imperfect.

content.html:

Model
x_distorted = x + [2*p1*x*y + p2*(r^2 + 2*x^2)]
y_distorted = y + [p1*(r^2 + 2*y^2) + 2*p2*x*y]
p1 and p2 capture asymmetric shifts due to lens decentering or tilt relative to the image plane.
Practical check
Estimate p1 and p2 during calibration and inspect whether undistorted images remove asymmetric shifts in corner positions.
Key Takeaway
Include tangential terms when mechanical alignment is imperfect; undistortion uses all estimated coefficients to restore geometric fidelity.

screens.title: Undistortion and Validation
screens.subtitle: Comparing original and undistorted images to confirm calibration

narration.text: Undistortion applies the estimated distortion coefficients and intrinsics to remap pixels so that geometric relationships in the scene are restored. The typical workflow is to take an original image, use undistortImage with the camera parameters, and then compare structured elements such as checkerboard lines or straight architectural edges. A concrete example: draw straight lines on the original image—if radial distortion is present they will curve near the edges—then undistort the image and verify those lines reappear straight. Quantitatively, reprojection error reports how well the estimated parameters predict observed corner positions; low mean error combined with visual straightening indicates a successful calibration. A common pitfall is relying only on reprojection error without visual checks because small numerical error can still hide localized distortions. The practical recommendation is to use both numerical statistics and image comparisons before trusting parameters for tasks like 3D reconstruction or visual odometry. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Undistortion
Visual comparison
Place the original and undistorted images side-by-side. Look for straightening of grids and alignment of edges. Small reprojection error plus clean visuals means parameters are reliable.
Checklist
  • Do straight lines appear straight after undistortion?
  • Is mean reprojection error within acceptable range for your task?
  • Were enough diverse views used during calibration?
Concrete example
Undistort a chessboard image and draw straight lines. If they line up with grid corners and edges, undistortion succeeded where radial bending was visible before.
Key Takeaway
Combine numerical reprojection metrics with visual checks to decide if a calibration is ready for use in geometric tasks.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Camera Geometry (1 of 2)
screens.subtitle: Essential definitions and formulas to keep

narration.text: Keep these core concepts handy as you work with cameras in robotics. First, the pinhole camera and perspective projection: u = f X over Z plus cx, and v = f Y over Z plus cy; this captures how apparent size scales with distance. Second, the intrinsic matrix K bundles focal length and principal point into a 3×3 operator used in homogeneous projections. Third, extrinsic parameters are R and t, which place the camera in the world and are necessary to transform world points into camera coordinates before projection. Use these three together in the full equation p_homogeneous = K [R | t] P_homogeneous. A frequent error is omitting the final division by depth when converting from homogeneous coordinates. Remember also that focal length in vision is typically expressed in pixels because it mixes optical focal length and pixel scale.

keyIdea.title: Core formulas
keyIdea.text: u = f X/Z + cx; K groups f and cx, cy; use K[R|t] to project world points into pixels.

content.html:

Pinhole projection
u = f X/Z + cx; v = f Y/Z + cy — size scales inversely with depth.
Intrinsic matrix K
K = [f 0 cx; 0 f cy; 0 0 1] groups internal camera properties.
Extrinsics [R|t]
R and t transform world coordinates into the camera frame before projection.
Summary

Combine K and [R|t] and normalize homogeneous coordinates to project world points for robotic perception. Validate with both numeric error and visual checks.

narration.text: Finish by remembering the calibration and distortion essentials. Camera calibration with a checkerboard yields K and distortion coefficients by minimizing reprojection error over many views. Use a variety of angles and distances during capture so the solver has information across the image plane. Radial distortion (k1, k2, k3) bends lines and is modeled as a polynomial in radius; tangential distortion (p1, p2) accounts for decentering. After calibration, undistort images and verify that straight lines become straight and that reprojection error is acceptably low. A practical assessment is to take a 3D point and project it using the recovered parameters, comparing the predicted pixel coordinates to observed feature locations. The final reminder: trust but verify—combine statistical error measures with visual inspection before relying on camera parameters for mapping or navigation.
